#CGPOWER #MAXHEALTH #POONAWALLA #MFSL #SBILIFE #DALBHARAT #HDFCBANK #COFFEEDAY #INDUSTOWER

9 investments. 9 different stories. 
9 convictions worth questioning.

“KKR exited” sounds like useful information.

But without knowing why KKR entered, what changed while it owned the stake, and why it eventually sold, it tells us surprisingly little.

The image shows the returns.
The stories are more interesting.

1. CGPOWER | The investment KKR never really chose

KKR did not enter CG Power as a conventional PE bet.

In September 2019, KKR’s credit entities ended up with ~10% of CG Power at ₹14.25/share by enforcing pledged shares against loans made to the promoter group.

And look at the situation then.

CG Power had just disclosed serious accounting and governance irregularities. 

Liabilities had been understated, related-party transactions were under investigation, operations were deteriorating and lenders were looking for a resolution.

So KKR’s “thesis” here was primarily credit recovery, not:
Power equipment is going to boom.

KKR sold during 2020.

Then Murugappa Group entered through Tube Investments, repaired the balance sheet, restored governance and rebuilt the operating business.

Today, the backdrop could barely look more different.

India is in another large transmission/grid-capex cycle, driven by electrification and renewable integration.

CG Power has also added an entirely new semiconductor adjacency through CG Semi, whose first facility started commercial production in 2026.

Post-KKR reference return: ~51x.

Questioning the conviction:
Can a terrible company situation temporarily hide a very good underlying industrial asset?

2. MAXHEALTH | Consolidation before healthcare became fashionable

KKR-backed Radiant moved on Max Healthcare in 2018.

The thesis was unusually explicit:
scale + consolidation + cost synergies + margin improvement + growing demand for quality healthcare.

The merger created one of India's largest hospital networks, with more than 3,200 beds at the time, and KKR specifically highlighted the ability to use the platform for further healthcare consolidation.

KKR eventually made roughly 5x and exited.

But that did not mean India's hospital runway had ended.

Max today operates 6,100+ beds, while large Indian hospital operators continued delivering >15% revenue and EBITDA growth in FY26 amid further capacity build-out.

Post-KKR: ~2.83x.

Questioning the conviction:
When PE has already made 5x, has the opportunity matured, or has the company merely moved from turnaround → scale → compounding?

P.S: I personally stay away from direct investments in healthcare sector.

3. POONAWALLA | Magma was originally a financial-inclusion bet

Go back to 2011.

Magma was not today's Poonawalla Fincorp.

It was an NBFC heavily exposed to rural and semi-urban India, financing commercial vehicles, construction equipment, tractors, cars and SMEs.

Around 80% of its branches were in rural/semi-urban markets.

I could not find a clean public KKR statement spelling out its exact thesis, but the contemporaneous investment documents make the likely thesis fairly clear:
underserved credit + branch expansion + product expansion + financial inclusion.

KKR exited around 2018 at roughly 2x.

Then the company itself changed.

New promoter. New balance sheet.
New distribution. New products. 
New underwriting architecture.

By FY26, Poonawalla Fincorp had ₹60,348 Cr AUM, up 69.4%, with a much broader mix across secured and unsecured products.

Post-KKR: ~2.68x.

Questioning the conviction:
In lending, what is the real moat?
Distribution? Cost of capital? 
Underwriting? Or the ability to reinvent all three?

4. MFSL | KKR explicitly bet on financialisation

KKR bought 9.95% of Max Financial in 2016 just after the Max Group demerger created a clean listed life-insurance vehicle.

KKR's rationale was explicit:
India's growth, increasing financial savings, and the resulting growth of the life-insurance industry.

That structural thesis largely played out.

But today's question is different.

IRDAI is now proposing another reset of insurance distribution economics, including tighter commission and expense structures.

Post-KKR reference: ~+120%.

Questioning the conviction:
If insurance penetration remains low but distribution economics change, who captures the next decade's value: bank, agent or platform?

5. SBILIFE | Distribution itself was an asset
KKR entered SBI Life in December 2016 at ₹460/share, shortly before its IPO.

The attraction was difficult to miss.

SBI Life combined a leading private insurer with access to the enormous SBI distribution network. 

Contemporary analysis highlighted its profitability, product mix and reach through SBI's banking franchise.

KKR subsequently monetised through multiple transactions.

Post-KKR reference: ~+77%.

Now the same industry faces a new question as regulators try to lower distribution costs.

Questioning the conviction:
In insurance, is a giant distribution network always an advantage, or does its value change when commissions themselves are regulated downward?

6. DALBHARAT | KKR bought cement when everyone could see oversupply

In 2010, Indian cement was dealing with massive capacity additions, falling utilisation and pricing pressure, particularly in southern India. Industry utilisation had already fallen sharply as new supply entered.

And KKR invested ₹750 Cr into Dalmia.

Why?
The money was explicitly meant for:
organic growth + inorganic growth + deleveraging.

Dalmia was restructuring itself into a focused cement platform, had reached 9 MTPA capacity and was planning another 10 MTPA of greenfield projects.

KKR eventually made 3.6x.

Post-KKR: ~+61%.

Questioning the conviction:
Is industry overcapacity always bearish?

Or can the weak part of a cycle actually be the best time for a low-cost player with capital to build capacity?

7. HDFCBANK | KKR wasn't just buying a mortgage lender

KKR invested in HDFC Ltd in early 2018.

But look at what the fresh capital was meant for:

→ maintain HDFC's stake in HDFC Bank
→ health-insurance opportunities
→ stressed real-estate assets
→ affordable housing
→ funding subsidiaries

It was effectively backing a capital-allocation platform, not merely a home-loan book.

Then came the NBFC liquidity crisis.

Years later came the HDFC Ltd + HDFC Bank merger.

KKR itself had already exited with roughly a 15% gain.

Post-KKR equivalent price return: ~+22%.

Questioning the conviction:
Was HDFC's historical moat the mortgage product itself, or the ecosystem, funding advantage and capital allocation around it?

That distinction matters even more after the merger.

8. COFFEEDAY | Right consumption thesis. Wrong balance-sheet outcome.

In 2010, KKR called Café Coffee Day a fast-growing retailer.

The consumer story was obvious.

India's organised retail market was expanding rapidly, CCD had built enormous brand recognition, and cafés were becoming part of urban India's changing consumption habits.

But KKR wasn't buying only a coffee shop.

The holding company also contained several other businesses, including real estate/infrastructure-related assets.

KKR monetised some shares at much higher prices, but remained invested while leverage and corporate complexity overwhelmed the consumer story.

Its eventual overall outcome was only around 1.2x.

Questioning the conviction:
Can you be completely right about the consumer trend and still lose because the capital structure is wrong?

Brand ≠ balance sheet.

9. INDUSTOWER | Telecom grew. The tower stock didn't compound accordingly.

KKR invested $250m in Bharti Infratel in 2008.
The setup was compelling.

India was adding telecom subscribers rapidly. Operators were expanding into new geographies. 

Sharing passive infrastructure allowed faster rollouts and better economics.

The tower model had significant operating leverage because each additional tenant could improve returns on an already-built asset.

KKR eventually made roughly 1.8x.

Yet the successor Indus Towers has delivered roughly flat-to-negative price returns from our exit reference, excluding substantial dividends.

Meanwhile the underlying infrastructure never became irrelevant.

Indus is still adding towers and co-locations, has 563,000 installed 5G BTSs, and its tenancy ratio stands around 1.62.

Questioning the conviction:
Can an industry experience exponential data growth while the infrastructure owner still delivers mediocre stock returns?

Absolutely.

Demand growth ≠ shareholder returns.
And that connects all nine stories.

KKR exiting is an event.
It is not an investment thesis.

PE investors have fund lives, return hurdles and liquidity constraints.

They also often own meaningful blocks.

So exits commonly happen through multiple block/bulk/open-market transactions, sometimes spread across months or years.

More importantly, KKR's investment objective and your investment objective can be completely different.

The better questions are:

Why did they enter?
What changed while they were there?
Why are they exiting?

And which part of the original thesis still has runway after they leave?

That, to me, is a much better way to exercise the #QuestioningConvictionMuscle than blindly following “smart money.”

India installed 8.2 GWh of grid batteries in the first half of 2026.

Nearly every cell inside them was imported.

Why does that matter?

Look at the demand side.
H1 2025: 98 MWh of battery storage installed.
H1 2026: 8.2 GWh.

That's 84 times in one year.
Crisil expects another 45 to 50 GWh to be commissioned across FY27 and FY28. Wood Mackenzie puts India's storage tender pipeline at 260 GWh.

Now the supply side.
In August, Wood Mackenzie counted 2 GWh of operational cell capacity in India. That's enough to meet less than 1% of the pipeline. Even with Exide's new 6 GWh line, which isn't in commercial production yet, domestic supply is a small fraction of what's coming.

So the gap gets filled by imports.
🔹 Li-ion battery imports in FY26: $4.7 bn, up 57%
🔹 Share from China: 83.6%

And this isn't just a trade deficit number. It shows up in P&Ls.

Chinese storage cell prices rose 22% in six months. Crisil says battery costs went from $50 to 55/kWh in 2025 to $70 to 75/kWh in 2026.

Developers usually buy batteries about a year after winning a bid. So projects won at 2025 tariffs are now paying 2026 prices. Crisil flags 12 GWh of capacity with weak returns.

When one country supplies your cells, it also sets your margins.

That's why local manufacturing matters.  For pricing power.

India has announced 226 GWh of cell capacity through 2035. 

Here's the part most people miss.
In July 2025, Beijing added LFP cathode technology to its restricted-export list. Taking it out of China now needs a licence.

On paper, that covers one material. On the ground, Indian companies are telling a very different story.

Amara Raja signed a licence with Gotion's European arm in 2024. It never moved. The company is now building its own tech, and its new-energy head says sharing is "largely discouraged by the Chinese government."

Then came the part that made me stop.

This week, Advait signed to buy up to 1 GWh of cells from China's Hithium. Back in January, Bloomberg reported that Hithium wouldn't license its LFP tech to Reliance. Reliance denied it.

So China will sell India the cell. Just not the recipe.

JSW has stopped waiting for it.

Last week, chairman Sajjan Jindal called the cell "the new oil" and said China will supply cells but won't share the know-how. His own estimate for building the technology in-house: one to two years, if things go well.

Also, JSW Projects and COEP Tech announced a battery R&D centre in Pune, with over ₹800 crore committed across two phases. Phase 1 will design and prototype lithium-ion and sodium-ion cells. Phase 2 is a validation centre able to produce cells from 100 to 600 Ah.

And Exide? Its 6 GWh plant was commissioned last week on SVOLT technology. But that deal was signed in March 2022, three years before the door closed.

Where India's own effort stands:
🔹 PLI ACC scheme: 40 GWh awarded, ~1.4 GWh operational, zero incentives paid as of Feb 2026
🔹 Ola Electric: 2.5 GWh operational, in-house technology
🔹 Amara Raja: first 2 GWh line targeted for 2027
🔹 Agratas (Tata): 20 GWh at Sanand, first equipment arrived this month, output in 2027

If the lock sits on the cathode, the materials layer is where it gets interesting:
🔹 Gujarat Fluorochemicals: supplying LiPF6 commercially since Dec 2025. LFP cathode final qualification expected by Q3 FY27
🔹 Himadri Speciality: 40,000 tpa LFP cathode in Phase I, first 2,000 tpa by Q3 FY27
🔹 Neogen Chemicals: ₹1,795 cr battery-chemicals capex, electrolyte production in H1 FY27

🔸 The other side: restricted is not banned, and licences can still be granted. Home-grown cells cost 25 to 40% more than imports. 

And China's wider controls on anode, cathode and cell-making equipment are only suspended, until 10 Nov 2026.

India can announce gigawatts. Buying the recipe is getting harder.

Why interest rates and earnings growth matter so much when judging index valuations.
To understand this more applicable way is to look at Nifty valuation is through the "equity risk premium" ! 
At around 19–20x PE, Nifty earnings yield is roughly 5–5.2%.
India’s 10-year bond yield is around 6–7%.
So purely on current yield, equities are not giving you any obvious premium over bonds, & the extra return has to come from future earnings growth.
If Nifty earnings grow 12–14% for the next few years, this can still work well because your earnings base keeps expanding, but if earnings growth drops to 6–8%, suddenly the present valuation starts looking far less attractive.

Srirangam, 1323. The year the temple emptied.

The Koyil Olugu is the chronicle the Ranganathaswamy temple kept of itself. It is the source for what follows. Not a modern reconstruction. The temple's own record of its own worst year. Malik Kafur had already been through the Tamil country in 1311 and robbed Srirangam. In 1323 Ulugh Khan came back.

The Koyil Olugu records 12,000 Srivaishnavas at Srirangam. It records that 11,250 of them were killed.

Before the killing started the priests got the utsava murti of Ranganatha out. They carried the deity into the forests of Kerala, then up into the hills at Tirupati, where it stayed. The sanctum at Srirangam stood empty for ~60 years.

Think about what that means as a fact of ordinary life. 3 generations of a temple town where the god was not at home. Children born, married and buried at Srirangam who never saw the deity in its own sanctum.

In 1371 the Vijayanagara commanders brought Ranganatha back and put the deity in its place. Srirangam is the largest functioning temple complex on earth. 156 acres. 7 concentric walls. 21 gopurams. It is not a ruin and it is not a museum, because the people who carried the deity out did not let it become one.

Go to Srirangam and stand in the sanctum. Then read the Koyil Olugu and work out what it cost to keep that sanctum occupied.

Owning a pucca house is a dream for every individual. During his election campaign in Bengal, Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri @narendramodi ji had mentioned the plight of Jute Mill workers and promised pucca houses for them if BJP government comes in power. To turn that promise into reality, our government, under the leadership of Hon’ble @SuvenduWB ji, has taken an initiative to provide affordable housing for jute mill workers.

At an important announcement was made in a Press Conference at the Labour Department today, it was decided to facilitate affordable housing for eligible EWS-category jute mill workers on a pilot basis in North 24 Parganas and Hooghly districts under the Affordable Housing in Partnership ( #AHP ) component of PMAY-Urban 2.0.

Eligible worker families with an annual household income of up to ₹3 lakh and who do not own a pucca house anywhere in the country will be eligible to benefit from this initiative.

Each housing unit will have a carpet area of 30–45 square metres (approximately 320–485 square feet), with at least two rooms, a kitchen and a toilet. The estimated construction cost of each flat will be approximately ₹5.50 lakh. Of this, ₹1.50 lakh will be contributed by the Central Government, ₹2.79 lakh by the State Government, and ₹50,000 by the beneficiary. The remaining approximately ₹71,000 will be borne by the Labour Welfare Board of the Labour Department.

In North 24 Parganas, Bhatpara, Titagarh and Kamarhati Municipalities have been directed to identify suitable and dispute-free government land for the project. In Hooghly, special camps will be organised with the assistance of the Labour Department and the Labour Commissionerate to help workers submit their applications. Around 8,000 #jute mill #workers have already expressed interest in this initiative.

The Labour Department will coordinate with the district administration, municipalities, workers’ organisations and mill managements to facilitate the identification of eligible beneficiaries and the application process.

The primary objective of this initiative is to improve the quality of life of jute mill workers and their families by providing them with safe, secure and dignified housing.

Carysil Ltd | Plant Visit & Management Meet Notes

We recently visited Carysil’s manufacturing facility in Bhavnagar, Gujarat, on 25th September 2026, as part of a site visit organised by Go India Advisors (@goindiastocks ).

The visit provided first-hand insights into Carysil’s manufacturing capabilities, capacity constraints, customer relationships, product innovation, India Growth strategy and its transition towards an integrated kitchen & bathroom solutions platform.

Here are some key takeaways: 👇

1. Capacity is increasingly becoming the key constraint

Quartz sinks remain the core business. The plant is operating at high utilisation(88%), with mould availability and carrier capacity emerging as practical bottlenecks. The company currently has 10 lakh annual quartz-sink capacity, with another 2.5 lakh units planned.

Stainless-steel sinks are even tighter: 2.5 lakh annual capacity is operating at ~91.6% utilisation, with another 1.5 lakh units of capacity planned.

2. Manufacturing integration is deepening

What stood out at the plant was the increasing level of in-house capability — from moulds, dies and tooling to press-shop operations, CNC machining, PVD finishing and appliance assembly.

Bringing more processes in-house should provide greater control over cost, lead times, product development and quality, while reducing dependence on external vendors.

3. Quartz has a strong global OEM franchise

The quartz business remains predominantly OEM-led, with the plant indicating roughly 80% OEM / 20% own-brand mix. Global relationships include customers such as IKEA, Home Depot, Lowe’s and other large kitchen retailers/brands.

An interesting opportunity is the combination of OEM scale + proprietary manufacturing capabilities + increasing own-brand presence.

4. India could become an important second growth engine

Management is pushing aggressively into India through brand stores, dealers, e-commerce, B2B and the Karesi brand.

Domestic revenue was ~₹178 Cr in FY26, with management targeting ₹500 Cr by FY29/FY30. The company also plans significant investment in brand stores, including 50–60 stores, while Karesi is being positioned to address the mid-segment without diluting Carysil’s premium positioning.

5. Product portfolio is expanding beyond sinks

Faucets, kitchen appliances, RO/water solutions and integrated kitchen offerings are being developed as the next growth vectors.

The stainless-steel faucet opportunity is particularly interesting as the company positions the products as lead-free, with manufacturing capabilities including CNC machining, drilling and PVD finishing.

6. Technology remains a key differentiator

The plant showcased multiple manufacturing routes across deep-drawn stainless-steel sinks, handmade sinks and PVD finishes, while the quartz business is built around formulation, mould-making, casting and finishing capabilities.

Management is also preparing to launch premium nano-technology products, aimed at improving product performance and differentiation.

7. The biggest near-term watchpoint is execution: Management is maintaining 15% CAGR guidance, while current challenges include container availability, freight and elevated input costs. Current expansion is expected to add 2.5 lakh sink capacity, followed by another ~₹300 Cr of CapEx over 5 years aimed at supporting ~₹1,000 Cr of incremental revenue.

Our key takeaway: The plant visit made the strategic transition visible on the ground — from a global sink/OEM manufacturer towards a vertically integrated, multi-category kitchen & bathroom solutions platform.

Capacity + technology + India brand-building + new categories will be the key variables to watch from here.

Every market recap is framing IRDAI's consultation paper as bad news for insurance distributors. I read it as the regulator finally doing something about a broken sales machine.

India's insurance penetration is 3.7% of GDP, less than half the global average of 7.3%. Yet IRDAI logged 26,600 mis-selling complaints in FY25 alone, up 14% from the year before. You do not fix low penetration by letting banks shove unsuitable policies down borrowers' throats to earn a fat commission.

The trigger for this is clear. IRDAI scrapped product-wise commission caps in 2023 for a broader expense ceiling. Insurers responded by competing aggressively for distributors, and some breached the limits. So now the regulator wants to pull the EoM ceiling down gradually over five years and simplify the whole distribution network into three categories.

Policybazaar and Turtlemint have fallen 30% since the news. I get why. Commission income is their business model, and less generosity from insurers means thinner margins.

But here is where I might be wrong. Cheaper distribution sounds great until you remember that good advice costs money. If commissions shrink too far, the pushy bank agent survives and the helpful advisor stops being viable. I am not sure IRDAI has cracked that part yet, and it worries me more than any stock price.

My bank tried to bundle insurance with a home loan once. I said no and got the loan anyway. If these rules pass, the next borrower might not need my stubbornness. Are you seeing this trend where you bank, or still getting the hard sell?

​1)Netweb Technologies: 

Doing end-to-end data center and cloud infrastructure setups. A less asset-heavy model. 62% of revenue is now coming from the AI segment, sitting on a ₹500 Cr order book. High repetition rate from clients (98%) and guiding for 30-40% growth.

​2)E2E Networks: 

An asset-heavy model where they build data centers (buying expensive NVIDIA GPUs) and rent out cloud computing capacity. Monthly recurring revenue is doubling YoY. Backed by a 21% stake from L&T.

​3)Aeroflex Industries: 

Shifting focus from traditional metal hoses for oil/gas to liquid cooling systems for AI data centers. Cooling skids are priced around ₹2.5-3 lakh each, and they are aggressively expanding capacity from 9,000 to 15,000 skids by Q3 FY27.

​2] Electronics Manufacturing Services (EMS)

2.1)​Syrma SGS: 

Guiding for 35% growth. FY28 looks even stronger as their new PCB assembly facility comes online. Shifting focus away from low-margin box builds toward high-margin ODM models.

2.2)​Amtron Electronics (SME):

Operating in high-margin segments (medical, EV tech, AI, aerospace) yielding an industry-leading 22-23% EBITDA margin.

​3] Electronics Retailing

​3.1)Aditya Vision (AVL):

Dominating the Hindi heartland (Bihar, UP, Jharkhand) and now expanding into Chhattisgarh, MP, and West Bengal. Consistent 25-30 store additions yearly with strong 10-11% margins.

3.2)​Electronics Mart India (EMI): 

A turnaround story. The initial drag from their North India (Delhi/NCR) expansion is breaking even, boosting consolidated margins.

​3.3)GNG Electronics:

Capitalizing on the supply-demand gap in the refurbished/used laptop market. Average selling prices are moving up from ₹25k to over ₹30k, expanding PAT margins.

​4] Platform Businesses

4.1)​CarTrade Tech: 

A brilliant asset-light platform model. The OLX acquisition is turning into a game-changer for them, driving high-margin subscriptions via the Elite Buyer program (adding 5,000+ daily). Management is guiding for ₹1,000 Cr PAT by FY30.
​Paytm: UPI MDR charge structures and cross-selling (loans, broking, MTF) are providing tailwinds. Management aiming to push EBITDA margins from 8% to the 15-20% range.

4.2)Eternal (​Zomato & Blinkit):

Blinkit has hit EBITDA breakeven and is narrowing losses rapidly.They are growing via margin preservation rather than heavy discounting, making them the clear leader in quick commerce.

​4.3)Nykaa: 

Beauty (70% of revenue) continues to thrive as international brands prefer listing on their platform rather than spending massive CAPEX on physical retail.

​4.4)urum PropTech:

Transitioning from loss-making to reporting positive PAT over the last three quarters. The https://t.co/GodTKOJTdV acquisition consolidates the real estate discovery ecosystem.

​5] Clean Energy

​5.1)Acme Solar: 

Shifting into Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to capture peak evening electricity prices (₹8-10 vs ₹4-5 daytime). Expanding BESS capacity from 3-4 GW to 10 GW by FY27 & 25 GW by FY30.

​5.2)CleanMax: 

Capturing industrial & AI data center demand, with AI contributing 40-45% of revenues. (Monitorable: grid curtailment issues in Rajasthan).

​6] Defense & Aerospace

6.1)​MTAR : 

Diversified across clean energy (Fuel cells for Bloom Energy make up 60% of revenue), nuclear reactors, and now data centers. Guiding for 80% revenue growth at 24% margins.

​6.2)IdeaForge: 

A pure play on the structural shift toward drone warfare. Order book is massive, but execution pace and margin pressure are the key monitorables.

​6.3)Apollo Micro Systems:

Getting into underwater & land mines alongside aerospace components. 40-50% growth guidance, though execution remains a tracking point.

कंपनी द्वारा बेचा जाने वाला प्रत्येक component RDSO certification की regulatory requirement से गुजरता है। यह certification एक महत्वपूर्ण entry barrier बनाता है, क्योंकि केवल approved vendors ही इन safety-critical railway components की supply कर सकते हैं।

RDSO Certification — मुख्य entry barrier

RDSO यानी Research Designs & Standards Organisation, Indian Railways की प्रमुख standards organisation है।

कंपनी के पास Class ‘A’ certification है, जिसे highest foundry grade के रूप में प्रस्तुत किया गया है। इसके अलावा कंपनी के पास:

ISO 9001 — Quality Management
ISO 14001 — Environmental Management
ISO 45001 — Occupational Health & Safety

जैसे certifications भी हैं।

महत्वपूर्ण बात यह है कि RDSO approval केवल एक बार मिलने वाली औपचारिकता नहीं है। नए competitors को भी इसी approval process को पूरा करना पड़ता है, जिसके कारण safety-critical railway component segment में entry आसान नहीं है।
